title: The song of Moses and the Lamb (Revelation 15–16)
word: The song of Moses and the Lamb
hook: by a sea of glass, they sing: great and marvelous are your works

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harvest, and a voice saying the dead in the Lord rest, with their works following them. Your line was they rest from their labors. Whose work did you carry a little further? Day one thousand three hundred seven.

On the far shore of the Red Sea, the water has just closed behind them. Under it, the army that chased them. Ahead, a desert. And Moses and the people of Israel sing. "I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." Miriam picks up a tambourine and the women dance. Now jump to near the end of the Bible. John sees another sea, made of glass and shot through with fire. People are standing on it, harps in their hands. They've come through their own long chase. And they sing too. Today's word is what they sing.
screen: `A SEA OF GLASS, MINGLED WITH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Revelation fifteen calls it "the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb." One song, two names. First, the old song comes back. Two days ago the beast's crowd borrowed a line from it; here it's sung to God again. Israel sang after God brought them through the sea out of slavery. The people on the glass sea sing after the Lamb has brought them through. John hears the Exodus story and the story of Jesus as one song. Second, the words. In the King James: "Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints." Listen to who the song is about. Not the singers. Not what they survived, or how brave they were. Every line is about God. Third, the song looks outward: "for all nations shall come and worship before thee." They've just escaped, and they're already singing about everybody else coming in. Fourth, what happens next is hard. In chapter sixteen, seven angels pour out bowls, and the plagues sound like Egypt again: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, and even unclean spirits like frogs. Some readers hear Revelation telling the Exodus story one more time, on a bigger stage. And twice the text says the people under the plagues still would not repent. So the song isn't sung because life is easy. It's sung on the shore, between the chase and the desert. In Acts, Paul and Silas do the same thing, singing praises in a prison at midnight. Praise, in this story, isn't a reward for things going well. It's what the rescued do on the shore.
screen: `SUNG BETWEEN THE CHASE AND THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing a song of praise. If you're somewhere you can, sing out loud. If not, hum, or let it play inside you. Pick a hymn you know, a psalm you've heard sung, or any song that says thank you for the world. Don't worry about your voice. The people by the glass sea had just come through something. Maybe you have too. Let the song be about what's great and good, not about you. If you pray, let it be your prayer. If you don't, just let it be a song. The bell holds the time.
The song of Moses and the Lamb. In Revelation fifteen, the song sung beside a sea of glass, echoing Israel's song at the Red Sea: great and marvelous are your works.
screen: `THE SONG OF MOSES AND THE LAMB — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: great and marvelous. Today, catch one thing worth praising, a sky, a meal, a kindness, and say so out loud, even just to yourself. Day one thousand three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Christians sing praise in worship, and some churches sing the words of Revelation 15:3–4 as a canticle; the song at the sea from Exodus 15 also has a place in Jewish morning prayers.

original.note: Greek: a song, an ode. the word for the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb in Revelation 15:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty song in heaven.
what it means: the song of the rescued, sung between danger and the desert, all about God and open to every nation.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 15 at the Red Sea, sung again, and the bowls of chapter 16 retelling the plagues of Egypt.
recall: the first and last Greek letters
